---
title: "Turning linguistic records into data"
---

What, exactly, is one datum in an acoustic study? This question asks us to specify the **unit of observation**, the entity represented by one row of the analysis table. A record, such as an audio file, may contain several candidate observations, and several records may contribute to one speaker-level summary. Thus file count does not determine sample size.

We make the unit of observation concrete with [Hillenbrand et al.'s (1995) study of American English vowels](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.411872). The study recorded 45 men, 48 women, and 46 children producing 12 vowels in /hVd/ words, measured duration and formant contours, and asked listeners to identify the intended vowels. The complete teaching table is the audited `phonTools::h95` table from package version 0.2-2.2 under the package's BSD-2-Clause license. One row is one /hVd/ vowel token from one speaker; each speaker contributes one token for each vowel. The package imputed 10 originally missing F2 values and 41 originally missing F3 values, so this table cannot be used to study the release's natural missingness. The [data record](../data/hillenbrand/README.md) gives the source, preprocessing, license, and checksum.

```{r}
#| label: load-hillenbrand
library(ggplot2)

vowels <- read.csv("data/hillenbrand/vowels-complete.csv")

stopifnot(
  nrow(vowels) == 1668L,
  length(unique(vowels$speaker_id)) == 139L,
  all(table(vowels$speaker_id) == 12L),
  !anyNA(vowels[c("duration_ms", "f0_hz", "f1_hz", "f2_hz", "f3_hz")]) # dqr-allow: reference-metadata
)

str(vowels)
```

## Unit and observation key

The **unit of observation** is the entity represented by one row. Here it is one vowel token, not one speaker and not one acoustic measurement considered apart from its token. We use **observation key** for the smallest set of columns that identifies a row. The pair

$$
\langle\text{speaker ID},\text{vowel}\rangle
$$

is the key in this table.

```{r}
#| label: check-hillenbrand-key
key_count <- nrow(unique(vowels[c("speaker_id", "vowel")]))
speaker_count <- length(unique(vowels$speaker_id))
vowel_count <- length(unique(vowels$vowel))

stopifnot(
  key_count == nrow(vowels),
  speaker_count < nrow(vowels),
  vowel_count == 12L
)

c(rows = nrow(vowels), keys = key_count,
  speakers = speaker_count, vowels = vowel_count)
```

The speaker identifier alone is not a key because it repeats once for each vowel. A unique row and an independent row are different notions: uniqueness says that two rows are not the same token, whereas repeated speaker identifiers tell us that several tokens share a talker.

## What aggregation removes

To see what aggregation changes, compare the token table with speaker-by-vowel means and vowel means. In this design, the first aggregation happens to preserve one row per speaker and vowel because there is one token in each cell. The second collapses `r speaker_count` speakers to one row per vowel.

```{r}
#| label: aggregate-hillenbrand
speaker_vowel <- aggregate(
  f1_hz ~ speaker_id + speaker_type + vowel,
  data = vowels,
  FUN = mean
)
vowel_mean <- aggregate(f1_hz ~ vowel, data = vowels, FUN = mean)

stopifnot(
  nrow(speaker_vowel) == nrow(vowels),
  nrow(vowel_mean) == vowel_count
)

c(token_rows = nrow(vowels),
  speaker_vowel_rows = nrow(speaker_vowel),
  vowel_mean_rows = nrow(vowel_mean))
```

Once we replace the speaker-specific rows with vowel means, the resulting table cannot show how speakers vary. That information has been removed before a statistical model sees the data.

## Raw tokens and summaries

The figure shows the raw F1 measurements for *heed* /i/ and *hid* /ɪ/ (`i` and `I` in the release). The paired lines preserve the fact that each speaker produced both vowels; the accent points are vowel means, not additional observations.

```{r}
#| label: plot-hillenbrand-units
#| fig-cap: "Each gray point is a vowel token; lines join tokens from the same speaker. Blue diamonds show means across speakers."
two_vowels <- subset(vowels, vowel %in% c("i", "I"))
two_vowels$vowel_label <- factor(
  two_vowels$vowel,
  levels = c("i", "I"),
  labels = c("heed /i/", "hid /ɪ/")
)
two_means <- aggregate(f1_hz ~ vowel_label, data = two_vowels, FUN = mean)

stopifnot(nrow(two_vowels) == 2L * speaker_count)

ggplot(two_vowels, aes(vowel_label, f1_hz, group = speaker_id)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey82", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_point(color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(
    data = two_means,
    aes(vowel_label, f1_hz),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "#2C7FB8", shape = 18, size = 3
  ) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "First formant (Hz)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Tokens and types

A **token** is an occurrence in a particular context; a **type** groups occurrences that the analysis treats as equivalent. The table contains `r nrow(vowels)` vowel tokens and `r vowel_count` vowel-category types. A study of within-category acoustic variation needs the tokens. A descriptive inventory of which categories were elicited may use the types.

The grouping follows from the linguistic question. The same principle holds for words: occurrences of *runs* are distinct tokens, one word-form type, and perhaps members of the lemma *run*. No representation is preferable without a target question.

## Measurement, analysis, and generalization

Before plotting or modeling, finish this sentence:

> One observation represents ______.

Then ask (i) which columns identify that observation, (ii) which speakers, items, words, documents, or languages repeat, (iii) which variation preprocessing has removed, and (iv) whether the design contains replication at the level of the intended claim.

For the present table, one observation represents one speaker's production of one vowel in an /hVd/ word. The response may be duration or a formant measurement, the key is speaker by vowel, and speaker is a repeated grouping variable. Because most speakers were raised in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, these data provide a benchmark for that sampled population rather than a population sample of all American English speakers.

The unit tells us what a row means, while the key tells us which row it is. The [next page](making-sense-of-data.qmd) uses these same records to align a comparison with a phonetic question.

## Test the distinction

1. Use the displayed code to verify how many rows belong to each speaker. Why does that make `speaker_id` an incomplete observation key?
2. Create a table with one row per speaker by averaging F1 across vowels. Which phonetic contrast does that aggregation remove?
3. Use the data to count the number of tokens and speakers in each `speaker_type`. Which count answers a question about productions, and which answers a question about talkers?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Every speaker contributes 12 rows, so `speaker_id` repeats and becomes a complete observation key only when paired with `vowel`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Averaging F1 across vowels leaves one row per speaker but removes the within-speaker vowel contrast that distinguishes productions such as /i/ and /ɪ/. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The table contains 324 tokens from 27 boys, 228 from 19 girls, 540 from 45 men, and 576 from 48 women; token counts answer questions about productions, whereas distinct-speaker counts answer questions about talkers. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
